scams.name: Taxi Bill-Switch and Counterfeit Change
scams.description:
Outside El Rodadero hotels and near Parque de los Novios at night, taxi drivers flag down tourists offering flat-rate fares. The price sounds fair — 10,000 to 15,000 pesos for a cross-city trip — and the driver appears friendly and professional throughout the ride.

At payment, you hand over a 20,000-peso note. The driver turns away briefly, then holds up a 2,000-peso note insisting that is what you gave him — your bill has been palmed and replaced in a smooth sleight-of-hand. In the counterfeit variant, you hand a 50,000-peso note and the driver returns it claiming it is fake or he has no change; the note he returns is a forgery, and you discover the switch only when a shop refuses the bill the next day.

Paying with exact change is the cleanest defense, but when you must hand over a large bill, announce the denomination aloud as you pass it — "twenty thousand pesos" — and maintain eye contact so any swap is harder to execute. Using InDriver, Didi, or Uber sets the fare digitally before you enter the car, removing the cash-exchange risk entirely.
scams.avoidance: Carry small bills (5,000 and 10,000 peso notes) and pay with exact change whenever possible State the denomination out loud as you hand it to the driver: 'Here is twenty thousand pesos' Agree on the fare before entering the taxi and have the exact amount ready Use ride-hailing apps like InDriver, Didi, or Uber where payment is handled digitally Familiarize yourself with Colombian bill denominations and security features before arriving — check returned bills for watermarks
scams.location: Taxis throughout Santa Marta, especially outside hotels in El Rodadero, the Centro Histórico, and near Parque de los Novios at night
scams.tldr: Santa Marta taxi drivers near El Rodadero and the Centro Histórico bill-switch 20,000-peso notes for 2,000-peso notes during payment, or swap genuine large bills for counterfeits during change, costing tourists 18,000–50,000 pesos per ride.

scams.name: Fake Police Document Inspection
scams.description:
Near Parque de los Novios and around the Centro Histórico, pairs of men approach tourists wearing uniforms that closely resemble official police attire. They flash badges quickly — too quickly to read the details — and frame the stop as a routine anti-counterfeit check targeting the area. The tone is official but not aggressive; they want you to comply, not to run.

Once you hand over your wallet, one man examines your passport while the other flips through your cash, pocketing bills while appearing to inspect denominations and watermarks. They issue a printed "receipt" and direct you to the police station to recover your money. At the station, real officers confirm no such inspection took place and the receipt is worthless.

Real Colombian police do not conduct roadside wallet inspections for counterfeit bills, so any officer making that request is a red flag — ask immediately for their photo ID and badge number before handing over anything. If they resist, suggest walking together to the nearest station to verify their identity; genuine officers will agree, imposters will not. Carry only a photocopy of your passport on your person and never surrender your actual wallet.
scams.avoidance: Leave your passport at the hotel safe and carry only a photocopy of the photo page and entry stamps If approached by supposed police, politely request to see their official photo ID and badge number Suggest walking to the nearest police station to verify their identity — real officers will agree, scammers will not Never hand over your wallet — if asked for ID, hold it yourself and let them look at it in your hands Call 123 (Colombian police emergency) to verify any officer's identity before complying with demands
scams.location: Streets around the Centro Histórico, Parque de los Novios, walkways near Taganga, and roads near popular tourist sites
scams.tldr: Plain-clothes men posing as police near Parque de los Novios demand to inspect tourists' wallets for counterfeit bills, pocket the cash during the inspection, and issue fake receipts worth nothing at a real police station.

scams.name: Beach Distraction Theft
scams.description:
On Santa Marta's most popular beaches — El Rodadero, Taganga, and Playa Blanca — teams of two to three people work the sand while tourists swim. One member passes near unattended bags posing as a vendor or casual beachgoer; another positions slightly away, watching for the owner's return and signaling when the coast is clear.

When you wade into the water, the first person creates or exploits a distraction — a radio playing, a beach ball thrown near your things, or a vendor engaging you in the shallows to keep your eyes off the shore. In the time it takes you to look away, your bag has been rifled and your phone, wallet, and camera are gone. The Tayrona park beaches see the same pattern: a vendor approach in the water occupies you while an accomplice works your towel on shore.

The only reliable defense is having nothing worth stealing on the sand. Bring only what you can carry into the water — a waterproof phone pouch, one bank card, and enough cash for the day — and leave everything else locked in the hotel. If you are traveling with someone, take turns swimming so one person always watches the belongings.
scams.avoidance: Never leave valuables unattended on the beach — bring only what you need for the day and leave everything else at the hotel Use a waterproof phone pouch that you can take into the water with you Take turns swimming with a travel companion so someone always watches the belongings Use a portable beach safe or lockbox that you can secure to a fixed object like a beach chair At Tayrona Park or Taganga, bring only essentials: cash for food, a cheap phone, and sunscreen
scams.location: Playa El Rodadero, Taganga Beach, Playa Blanca, and beach areas around Parque Nacional Natural Tayrona
scams.tldr: Coordinated teams at Playa El Rodadero and Taganga Beach use vendor approaches or staged distractions to rifle unattended bags while tourists are in the water, typically taking phones, wallets, and cameras in under two minutes.

scams.name: Scopolamine (Devil's Breath) Drink Spiking
scams.description:
In El Rodadero bars and through dating apps, a woman initiates friendly conversation and quickly offers to buy a round of drinks. The setting is normal — a busy bar, upbeat music — and the woman appears genuinely interested. The drink looks, smells, and tastes exactly as ordered.

Within twenty to forty minutes you feel unusually dizzy and disoriented. You comply with whatever is suggested — returning to your hotel, opening a safe, making transfers — with no resistance and no memory of doing so. You wake hours later with your wallet, phone, watch, laptop, and any cash gone. Scopolamine, known locally as burundanga, is colorless and odorless and can be dissolved in a drink, applied to a business card, or blown as powder. Colombia logs an estimated 50,000 scopolamine victims annually.

Never let a drink out of your sight and never accept one poured outside your view, but the most important rule is simpler. Do not bring strangers back to your hotel room, regardless of how the evening has gone. If you feel unexpectedly disoriented after a single drink, tell a trusted companion immediately and get to a safe location rather than continuing on your own.
scams.avoidance: Never accept drinks from strangers and never leave your drink unattended — get a new one if you stepped away Avoid bringing strangers to your hotel room, especially people met at bars or through dating apps Go out with trusted friends and watch out for each other — if someone seems suddenly out of it, get them to safety immediately Use drink covers or bottle toppers to prevent anything being dropped into your beverage If you feel suddenly disoriented after a drink, tell a trusted person immediately and get to a safe location
scams.location: Bars and nightclubs in El Rodadero, late-night establishments in the Centro Histórico, and encounters initiated through dating apps
scams.tldr: Women working El Rodadero bars and dating apps spike tourists' drinks with scopolamine — a colorless, odorless drug locally called burundanga — leaving victims fully compliant and memory-free while accomplices clear hotel rooms of phones, wallets, and laptops.

scams.name: Overpriced Unofficial Tour Guide
scams.description:
At the entrance to Parque Nacional Natural Tayrona and near Lost City trek departure points, men approach arriving tourists presenting themselves as knowledgeable local guides. They quote prices that sound fair — around 80,000 pesos for a full-day park experience — and project enough confidence and local knowledge to read as legitimate.

Once inside the park, the guide provides minimal information, rushes through the trails, and spends most of the time on his phone. When you reach the beaches, he declares the tour finished. You discover that self-guided entry costs only 20,000 pesos and licensed guides with official credentials charge 50,000–60,000 pesos through verified agencies. The Lost City trek is even more tightly controlled — only four authorized operators can legally run it, and anyone offering the trek outside those channels is operating unlicensed.

Research standard prices before you arrive and book through agencies with verified reviews on TripAdvisor or GetYourGuide. For the Lost City trek, book only with one of the four licensed operators — Expotur, Wiwa Tour, Turcol, or Magic Tour — and ask any guide to show their official credentials before you agree to their services. A genuine guide will have a laminated license and will not be offended by the request.
scams.avoidance: Book tours through licensed agencies with verified reviews on TripAdvisor, Google, or GetYourGuide For the Lost City trek, only book with one of the few licensed operators (Expotur, Wiwa Tour, Turcol, or Magic Tour) Ask for official guide credentials and verify them with the tourism office if in doubt Get a written agreement including the itinerary, inclusions, and refund policy before paying Research the standard price for any tour before arriving so you can spot both overcharging and suspiciously low offers
scams.location: Outside the entrance to Parque Nacional Natural Tayrona, Minca coffee farm tours, Lost City (Ciudad Perdida) trek departures, and around Santa Marta's harbor
scams.tldr: Unauthorized men posing as guides at Tayrona National Park and Lost City trek departures charge tourists 80,000-peso fees for brief, low-effort walks — while official self-guided entry costs 20,000 pesos and licensed tours run 50,000–60,000 pesos through registered agencies.

scams.name: Bird Poop and Bracelet Distraction Theft
scams.description:
Near the cathedral and around Parque de los Novios, teams of two to four people operate in rotation through the Centro Histórico. One member taps a passing tourist on the shoulder and points to a white substance on their jacket — bird poop, they say — looking genuinely concerned. Alternatively, a vendor steps beside you and ties a colorful bracelet on your wrist, calling it a free local gift.

In the bird-poop variant, a second "helpful" person immediately appears with napkins and starts dabbing at your jacket, positioning their hands near your pockets and bag. A third person behind you unzips your bag or lifts your phone while your attention is on the stain. In the bracelet variant, the vendor demands 50,000–100,000 pesos to remove it while the argument positions accomplices near your pockets. These teams run three to four operations per hour in the busiest parts of the historic center.

Both variants work by stopping you and pulling your attention downward or sideways. If anyone points out a stain on your clothing or attaches anything to your wrist, do not stop — keep walking and inspect the stain only after you have stepped into a shop or open public area. Wear your bag across your front through the Centro Histórico and keep your phone in a zipped inner pocket, not in your hand or a back pocket.
scams.avoidance: If someone points out a stain, do not stop — walk away to a safe area before inspecting your clothing Do not accept 'free' bracelets, flowers, or gifts from strangers — decline firmly and keep walking Wear your bag on your front in the Centro Histórico and keep your phone in a zipped inner pocket Travel with a companion when possible so someone can watch your back during unexpected interactions Be especially alert near the cathedral and Parque de los Novios where these teams operate most actively
scams.location: Centro Histórico around the cathedral, Parque de los Novios, beachfront promenades, and busy pedestrian streets near Rodadero
scams.tldr: Coordinated teams in Santa Marta's Centro Histórico spray a white substance on tourists' clothing or tie bracelets on wrists without consent, then steal from bags during the distraction or demand 50,000–100,000 pesos to remove the "free gift."

scams.name: Attempted Knifepoint Robbery Near Historic Center
scams.description:
The Centro Histórico and El Rodadero beachfront are well-patrolled and relatively safe for tourists after dark. The risk concentrates in the transitional blocks — the side streets between bars and hotels, the poorly lit stretches off the main tourist corridors, and the darker sections of the road toward Taganga.

Two young men step from a doorway, one with a knife. They state their demands plainly — phone, wallet, watch — and the exchange takes under sixty seconds. Hesitation or argument escalates the threat immediately. The robbery typically happens within a few blocks of a well-lit tourist area, when visitors assume the danger zone has already passed.

Route choice after dark is the core decision. Never walk on side streets in Santa Marta after dark — use Uber, InDriver, or a hotel-arranged taxi even for distances of two or three blocks. Stick to Carrera 1 and the Parque de los Novios area when walking at night, avoid displaying phones or cameras outside, and ask hotel staff which specific streets are safe before heading out.
scams.avoidance: Never walk on side streets in Santa Marta after dark — use Uber, InDriver, or a hotel-arranged taxi even for short distances Stick to well-lit, well-trafficked streets like Carrera 1 and the Parque de los Novios area when out at night Do not wear expensive jewelry, watches, or visible electronics when walking around the city If confronted, hand over your belongings without resistance — nothing is worth your safety Ask your hotel which specific streets are safe to walk at night and which to avoid
scams.location: Side streets off the Centro Histórico at night, dark streets near Taganga, and poorly lit areas between bars and hotels
scams.tldr: Pairs of young men rob tourists at knifepoint on poorly lit side streets off the Centro Histórico at night, taking phones, wallets, and watches in under a minute, with any hesitation or resistance escalating the threat immediately.
